\section{Declarations}

\begin{definition}[Encoded query membership]
\lean{Complexity.KarpLipton.Query}
\label{Complexity.KarpLipton.Query}
\leanok
\uses{BoolCircuit.CVAL, Turing.pairEncode}
For Boolean words $d,y,e$, the query holds exactly when the nested pair encoding of $d$,
$y$, and $e$ belongs to the language $\mathrm{CVAL}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Bad specification conditions]
\lean{Complexity.KarpLipton.BadSpec}
\label{Complexity.KarpLipton.BadSpec}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.KarpLipton.Query, Complexity.KarpLipton.dropMarker, Turing.pairEncode}
Let $C,c$ be natural numbers, let $V$ be a language of Boolean words, and let
$x,U,u,j,p$ be Boolean words. The bad-specification condition requires that
$|u|=C(|x|+1)^c$, $|j|\le C(|x|+1)^c$, and $|p|\le C(|x|+1)^c$, together with at least
one of the following: the query on the encoding of $x,u$ with the word obtained by
dropping the marker from $U$ and using a block of $C(|x|+1)^c$ true bits followed by
false fails; or $|p|=C(|x|+1)^c$, that query with false prepended to $p$ holds, and the
encoding of the pair $(x,u)$ with $p$ is not in $V$; or $|j|+|p|+1=C(|x|+1)^c$, the
query with $|j|$ true bits followed by true, false, and then $p$ holds, while the
queries with $|j|$ true bits followed by false and then $p$ with either false or true
appended both fail.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[First component of a nested encoding]
\lean{Complexity.KarpLipton.gx}
\label{Complexity.KarpLipton.gx}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.pairFstD}
For a Boolean word $z$, define $g(x)$ to be the first component obtained by applying the
first-component projection twice to $z$ under the pair encoding.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[First projection after second projection]
\lean{Complexity.KarpLipton.gU}
\label{Complexity.KarpLipton.gU}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.pairFstD, Complexity.pairSndD}
For a Boolean list $z$, define $g_U(z)$ by applying the second-component extraction to
the result of applying the first-component extraction to $z$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Nested first projection]
\lean{Complexity.KarpLipton.gu}
\label{Complexity.KarpLipton.gu}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.pairFstD, Complexity.pairSndD}
For a Boolean list $z$, define $g_u(z)$ by applying the first-component extraction twice
to the second-component extraction of $z$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Second projection after first projection]
\lean{Complexity.KarpLipton.gj}
\label{Complexity.KarpLipton.gj}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.pairFstD, Complexity.pairSndD}
For a Boolean list $z$, define $g_j(z)$ by applying the second-component extraction to
the first-component extraction of the second-component extraction of $z$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Nested second projection]
\lean{Complexity.KarpLipton.gp}
\label{Complexity.KarpLipton.gp}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.pairSndD}
For a Boolean list $z$, define $g_p(z)$ by applying the second-component extraction
twice to $z$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Nested first projection of a paired input]
\lean{Complexity.KarpLipton.gx_pair}
\label{Complexity.KarpLipton.gx_pair}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.KarpLipton.gx, Turing.pairEncode}
\difficulty{1}
For bit strings $x,U,t,u,j,p$, let $\langle a,b\rangle$ denote the encoding obtained by
doubling each bit of $a$, appending the separator $01$, and then appending $b$. Applying
the total first projection twice to $\langle\langle x,U\rangle,t\rangle$ returns $x$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Extracting the second component of a nested pair]
\lean{Complexity.KarpLipton.gU_pair}
\label{Complexity.KarpLipton.gU_pair}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.KarpLipton.gU, Turing.pairEncode}
\difficulty{1}
For any bit strings $x,U,t$, decode the outer pair whose first component is the encoding
of $(x,U)$ and whose second component is $t$, then take the second component of the
decoded inner pair. The result is $U$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Nested first projection of a paired string]
\lean{Complexity.KarpLipton.gu_pair}
\label{Complexity.KarpLipton.gu_pair}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.KarpLipton.gu, Turing.pairEncode}
\difficulty{1}
For bit strings $x,U,t,u,j,p$, let $\langle a,b\rangle$ denote the encoding obtained by
doubling each bit of $a$, appending the separator $01$, and then appending $b$. Applying
the total first projection twice to the total second projection of $\langle\langle
x,U\rangle,\langle\langle u,j\rangle,p\rangle\rangle$ returns $u$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Extracting the index component of a nested pair]
\lean{Complexity.KarpLipton.gj_pair}
\label{Complexity.KarpLipton.gj_pair}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.KarpLipton.gj, Turing.pairEncode}
\difficulty{1}
For any bit strings $x,U,t,u,j,p$, form the pair whose first component is the encoding
of $(x,U)$ and whose second component is the encoding of the pair consisting of $(u,j)$
and $p$. The second component of the decoded pair within that second component is $j$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Second nested projection of a paired string]
\lean{Complexity.KarpLipton.gp_pair}
\label{Complexity.KarpLipton.gp_pair}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.KarpLipton.gp, Turing.pairEncode}
\difficulty{1}
For bit strings $x,U,t,u,j,p$, let $\langle a,b\rangle$ denote the encoding obtained by
doubling each bit of $a$, appending the separator $01$, and then appending $b$. Applying
the total second projection twice to $\langle\langle x,U\rangle,\langle\langle
u,j\rangle,p\rangle\rangle$ returns $p$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Polynomial-Time Computability of the Iterated First Projection]
\lean{Complexity.KarpLipton.polyTimeComputable_gx}
\label{Complexity.KarpLipton.polyTimeComputable_gx}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.KarpLipton.gx, Complexity.PolyTimeComputable, Complexity.PolyTimeComputable.comp, Complexity.polyTimeComputable_pairFstD}
\difficulty{1}
The function on finite binary strings that takes the first component of a string parsed
as a self-delimiting pair and then takes the first component of the result, using the
empty string whenever either required parse fails, is polynomial-time computable.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Polynomial-Time Computability of Nested Projection]
\lean{Complexity.KarpLipton.polyTimeComputable_gU}
\label{Complexity.KarpLipton.polyTimeComputable_gU}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.KarpLipton.gU, Complexity.PolyTimeComputable, Complexity.PolyTimeComputable.comp, Complexity.polyTimeComputable_pairFstD, Complexity.polyTimeComputable_pairSndD}
\difficulty{1}
Define $g(z)=\pi_2(\pi_1(z))$, where $\pi_1$ and $\pi_2$ are the total first and second
projections of the aligned pair parser, each returning the empty string when the input
does not parse as a pair. Then $g$ is polynomial-time computable.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Polynomial-Time Computability of the First Projection Composition]
\lean{Complexity.KarpLipton.polyTimeComputable_gu}
\label{Complexity.KarpLipton.polyTimeComputable_gu}
\leanok

\difficulty{1}
The function on finite binary strings that first takes the second component of a string
parsed as a self-delimiting pair, then takes the first component of that result, and
then takes its first component again—using the empty string whenever a required parse
fails—is polynomial-time computable.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Polynomial-Time Computability of Triple Projection]
\lean{Complexity.KarpLipton.polyTimeComputable_gj}
\label{Complexity.KarpLipton.polyTimeComputable_gj}
\leanok

\begin{theorem}[Polynomial-Time Computability of Repeated Projection]
\lean{Complexity.KarpLipton.polyTimeComputable_gp}

\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Membership in the Bad Language]
\lean{Complexity.KarpLipton.mem_badLang}
\label{Complexity.KarpLipton.mem_badLang}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.KarpLipton.BadSpec, Complexity.KarpLipton.badLang, Complexity.KarpLipton.gU, Complexity.KarpLipton.gj, Complexity.KarpLipton.gp, Complexity.KarpLipton.gu, Complexity.KarpLipton.gx}
\difficulty{1}
For natural numbers $C$ and $c$, a language $V$ of bit strings, and a bit string $z$,
membership of $z$ in the language defined by the bad-specification predicate is
equivalent to that predicate holding for the five bit strings obtained by applying the
prescribed nested pair-decoding projections to $z$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Polynomial-Time Circuit Satisfiability Queries]
\lean{Complexity.KarpLipton.pred_query}
\label{Complexity.KarpLipton.pred_query}
\leanok
\uses{BoolCircuit.CVAL_mem_P, Complexity.KarpLipton.Query, Complexity.P, Complexity.PolyTimeComputable, Complexity.PolyTimeComputable.pairEncode, Complexity.preimage_mem_P}
\difficulty{1}
Let $d,y,e$ be polynomial-time computable functions from finite binary strings to finite
binary strings. The language of strings $z$ for which the pair encoding $\\langle d(z),
\\langle y(z),e(z)\\rangle\\rangle$ is a yes-instance of circuit satisfiability belongs
to $\\mathsf{P}$; here a yes-instance encodes a fan-in-two Boolean circuit together with
an input on which the circuit evaluates to true.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Polynomial-Time Length Equality Language]
\lean{Complexity.KarpLipton.pred_len_eq}

\uses{Complexity.KarpLipton.gx, Complexity.KarpLipton.polyTimeComputable_gx, Complexity.P, Complexity.PolyHierarchy.unaryPT_poly, Complexity.PolyTimeComputable, Complexity.lenEq_preimage_mem_P}

\begin{theorem}[Polynomial-time closure for the bad-specification language]
\lean{Complexity.KarpLipton.badLang_mem_P}
\label{Complexity.KarpLipton.badLang_mem_P}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.KarpLipton.badLang, Complexity.KarpLipton.dropMarker, Complexity.KarpLipton.gU, Complexity.KarpLipton.gj, Complexity.KarpLipton.gp, Complexity.KarpLipton.gu, Complexity.KarpLipton.gx, Complexity.KarpLipton.polyTimeComputable_dropMarker, Complexity.KarpLipton.polyTimeComputable_gU, Complexity.KarpLipton.polyTimeComputable_gj, Complexity.KarpLipton.polyTimeComputable_gp, Complexity.KarpLipton.polyTimeComputable_gu, Complexity.KarpLipton.polyTimeComputable_gx, Complexity.KarpLipton.pred_and, Complexity.KarpLipton.pred_len_eq, Complexity.KarpLipton.pred_len_le, Complexity.KarpLipton.pred_not, Complexity.KarpLipton.pred_or, Complexity.KarpLipton.pred_query, Complexity.P, Complexity.PolyHierarchy.unaryPT_poly, Complexity.PolyTimeComputable, Complexity.PolyTimeComputable.append, Complexity.PolyTimeComputable.comp, Complexity.PolyTimeComputable.pairEncode, Complexity.polyTimeComputable_const, Complexity.polyTimeComputable_prepend, Complexity.polyTimeComputable_unary, Complexity.preimage_mem_P, Turing.pairEncode}
\difficulty{5}
Let $C$ and $c$ be natural numbers, and let $V$ be a language of bit strings
in $P$. Form the language of strings $z$ for which the five decoded components
$x,U,u,j,p$ satisfy the following: $|u|=C(|x|+1)^c$, $|j|\le C(|x|+1)^c$, and $|p|\le

marker-deleted $U$, queried on $\varnothing x,u\varnothing$ with the all-ones marker of length
$C(|x|+1)^c$ followed by $0$, rejects; or $|p|=C(|x|+1)^c$, that circuit accepts the
query with suffix $0p$, and $\varnothing\varnothing x,p\varnothing$ is not in $V$; or $|j|+|p|+1=C(|x|+1)^c$, the
circuit accepts the query with suffix $1 0 p$ preceded by $|j|$ ones, and rejects both
queries with suffixes $0(p0)$ and $0(p1)$ preceded by $|j|$ ones. Then this language is
in $P$.

\begin{definition}[Inner language]
\lean{Complexity.KarpLipton.innerLang}
\label{Complexity.KarpLipton.innerLang}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.KarpLipton.badLang, Turing.pairEncode}
For natural numbers $C$ and $c$ and a language $V$ of Boolean lists, define the language
of Boolean lists $w$ such that, for every Boolean list $t$, the encoded pair $(w,t)$
does not belong to the bad-specification language determined by $C$, $c$, and $V$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Pair membership in the inner language]
\lean{Complexity.KarpLipton.mem_innerLang_pair}
\label{Complexity.KarpLipton.mem_innerLang_pair}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.KarpLipton.BadSpec, Complexity.KarpLipton.gU_pair, Complexity.KarpLipton.gx_pair, Complexity.KarpLipton.innerLang, Complexity.KarpLipton.mem_badLang, Turing.pairEncode}
\difficulty{4}
Let $C,c$ be natural numbers, let $V$ be a language of bit strings, and let $x,U$ be bit
strings. Write $B=C(|x|+1)^c$, and say that a query $(d,y,e)$ succeeds when the encoding
of $d$ paired with the encoding of $y$ and $e$ belongs to the circuit-satisfiability
language. The encoding of $x$ paired with $U$ belongs to the language of strings $w$
such that every bit string $t$ has the encoding of $w$ paired with $t$ outside the bad
language if and only if, for every three bit strings $u,j,p$, all of the following bad
cases are absent: $|u|=B$, $|j|\le B$, and $|p|\le B$, together with either (i) the
query with data $U$ after marker removal, input the encoding of $x$ paired with $u$, and
certificate consisting of $B$ ones followed by zero fails; (ii) $|p|=B$, that query with
certificate beginning with zero followed by $p$ succeeds, and the encoding of $x$ paired
with $u$, then paired with $p$, is outside $V$; or (iii) $|j|+|p|+1=B$, the query with
certificate consisting of $|j|$ ones followed by $1,0,p$ succeeds, and both queries with
certificates consisting of $|j|$ ones followed respectively by $0,p,0$ and $0,p,1$ fail.
\end{theorem}

\lean{Complexity.KarpLipton.innerLang_mem_coNP}

\difficulty{5}
Let $C,c\in\mathbb{N}$ and let $V$ be a language of bit strings belonging to
$\mathrm{P}$. The language consisting of those bit strings $w$ for which, for every bit
string $t$, the pairing of $w$ and $t$ does not belong to the language defined by the
bad-specification condition with parameters $C,c,V$ belongs to $\mathrm{coNP}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Witness existence from good specifications]
\lean{Complexity.KarpLipton.exists_witness_of_allGood}
\label{Complexity.KarpLipton.exists_witness_of_allGood}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.KarpLipton.BadSpec, Complexity.KarpLipton.Query, Complexity.KarpLipton.dropMarker, Turing.pairEncode}
\difficulty{6}
Let $C$ and $c$ be natural numbers, let $V$ be a language of bit strings, and
let $x,U$ be bit strings. Suppose that for every triple of bit strings $u',j,p$, the
length bounds $|u'|=C(|x|+1)^c$, $|j|\le C(|x|+1)^c$, and $|p|\le C(|x|+1)^c$ do not
hold together with any of the three bad cases: the corresponding circuit query rejects
the all-ones marker; or $|p|=C(|x|+1)^c$ and the query on $0p$ accepts while $\varnothing\varnothing
x,p\varnothing$ is not in $V$; or $|j|+|p|+1=C(|x|+1)^c$, the query on $1 0 p$ preceded by $|j|$
ones accepts, and both queries on $0(p0)$ and $0(p1)$ preceded by $|j|$ ones reject.
Then for every $u$ of length $C(|x|+1)^c$, there is a string $v$ of that length such
that $\varnothing\varnothing x,u\varnothing,v\varnothing$ belongs to $V$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Circuit query and family language equivalence]
\lean{Complexity.KarpLipton.query_iff_mem_language}

Let $F$ be a family of Boolean circuits such that every circuit in the family has fan-in
at most two, and let $y,e$ be binary strings. The pair encoding of $y$ and $e$ belongs

circuit $F$ on inputs of length $|\langle y,e\rangle|$, together with $y$ and $e$,

\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Query length]
\lean{Complexity.KarpLipton.qlen}
\label{Complexity.KarpLipton.qlen}
\leanok
For natural numbers $C$ and $c$ and a Boolean list $x$, define its query length to be
$2(2|x|+2+C(|x|+1)^c)+2+(C(|x|+1)^c+1)$, where $|x|$ is the length of $x$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Length of a nested pair encoding]
\lean{Complexity.KarpLipton.length_query}
\label{Complexity.KarpLipton.length_query}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.KarpLipton.qlen, Turing.length_pairEncode, Turing.pairEncode}
\difficulty{1}
Let $C,c$ be natural numbers and let $x,u,e$ be bit strings. If $|u|=C(|x|+1)^c$ and
$|e|=C(|x|+1)^c+1$, then $|\langle\langle x,u\rangle,e\rangle|=q(C,c,x)$, where

\begin{theorem}[Good circuit decisions exclude bad specifications]
\lean{Complexity.KarpLipton.allGood_of_decides}
\label{Complexity.KarpLipton.allGood_of_decides}
\leanok
\uses{BoolCircuit.DAGCircuit.encode, BoolCircuit.DAGCircuitFamily, BoolCircuit.DAGCircuitFamily.HasFaninTwo, BoolCircuit.DAGCircuitFamily.language, Complexity.KarpLipton.BadSpec, Complexity.KarpLipton.Query, Complexity.KarpLipton.dropMarker, Complexity.KarpLipton.length_query, Complexity.KarpLipton.mem_prefixLang_iff, Complexity.KarpLipton.prefixLang, Complexity.KarpLipton.qlen, Complexity.KarpLipton.query_iff_mem_language, Complexity.KarpLipton.wLen_pairEncode, Turing.pairEncode}

Let $C$ and $c$ be natural numbers, let $V$ be a language of bit strings, and
let $F$ be a family of acyclic Boolean circuits with at most two inputs per gate, with

bit strings $x,U$, suppose deleting the marker from $U$ gives the encoding of the
circuit in $F$ on input length $2(2|x|+2+C(|x|+1)^c)+2+(C(|x|+1)^c+1)$. Suppose also
that for every $u$ of length $C(|x|+1)^c$ there is a $v$ of that same length with $\varnothing\varnothing
x,u\varnothing,v\varnothing\text{ belongs to }V$. Then for every bit strings $u,j,p$ it is not the case
that all three length bounds $|u|=C(|x|+1)^c$, $|j|\le C(|x|+1)^c$, $|p|\le C(|x|+1)^c$
hold together with at least one of these: the corresponding circuit query on $\varnothing x,u\varnothing$
rejects the all-ones marker; $|p|=C(|x|+1)^c$ and the query on $0p$ accepts while $\varnothing\varnothing
x,p\varnothing
otin V$; or $|j|+|p|+1=C(|x|+1)^c$, the query on $1 0 p$ preceded by $|j|$ ones accepts,
and both queries formed by preceding $0(p0)$ and $0(p1)$ by $|j|$ ones reject. Here $\varnothing
a,b\varnothing$ denotes the encoding of a pair, and each query uses the circuit code obtained by
deleting the marker from $U$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Polynomial bound on circuit encoding length]
\lean{Complexity.KarpLipton.length_encode_le}
\label{Complexity.KarpLipton.length_encode_le}
\leanok
\uses{BoolCircuit.DAGCircuit.encode, BoolCircuit.DAGCircuit.length_encode_le_of_isFaninTwo, BoolCircuit.DAGCircuit.size, BoolCircuit.DAGCircuitFamily, BoolCircuit.DAGCircuitFamily.HasFaninTwo, Complexity.KarpLipton.qlen}
\difficulty{5}
Let $C,c,a,k$ be natural numbers and let $F$ be a family of directed acyclic circuits,
with the circuit in the family for inputs of length $n$ having $n$ input vertices.
Suppose every circuit in $F$ is well formed with fan-in at most two, and its size is at
most $a(n+1)^k$ for every $n\in\mathbb{N}$. Then for every bit string $x$, the encoding
length of the circuit in $F$ for inputs of length $q(C,c,x)$, plus one, is at most
$\bigl(12a^2(8+3C)^{2k}+1\bigr)(|x|+1)^{2(c+1)k}$, where
$q(C,c,x)=2\bigl(2|x|+2+C(|x|+1)^c\bigr)+2+C(|x|+1)^c+1$.
\end{theorem}

\uses{BoolCircuit.DAGCircuit.encode, BoolCircuit.PPoly, Complexity.KarpLipton.allGood_of_decides, Complexity.KarpLipton.exists_witness_of_allGood, Complexity.KarpLipton.innerLang, Complexity.KarpLipton.innerLang_mem_coNP, Complexity.KarpLipton.length_encode_le, Complexity.KarpLipton.mem_innerLang_pair, Complexity.KarpLipton.prefixLang_mem_NP, Complexity.KarpLipton.qlen, Complexity.NP, Complexity.PiP, Complexity.SigmaP, Complexity.mem_PiP_two_iff_forall_exists, Complexity.mem_SigmaP_two_iff}
\difficulty{5}
Suppose every language in NP is decidable by a family of fan-in-two Boolean circuits
whose sizes are bounded by a polynomial in the input length. Then every language in
$\Pi_2^P$ belongs to $\Sigma_2^P$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Collapse of the polynomial hierarchy to level two]
\lean{Complexity.PH_eq_SigmaP_two_of_NP_subset_PPoly}
\statementsource{Yap83}{
  pdf-1a201b302069-p003-b001,
  pdf-1a201b302069-p003-b006
}
\label{Complexity.PH_eq_SigmaP_two_of_NP_subset_PPoly}
\leanok
\uses{BoolCircuit.PPoly, Complexity.NP, Complexity.PH, Complexity.PH_eq_SigmaP_of_PiP_subset_SigmaP, Complexity.PiP_two_subset_SigmaP_two_of_NP_subset_PPoly, Complexity.SigmaP}
\difficulty{1}
Suppose every language in $\mathrm{NP}$ has polynomial-size Boolean circuit families
with fan-in at most two that decide it. Then the polynomial hierarchy $\mathrm{PH}$
equals $\Sigma_2^P$.
\end{theorem}
